Real wiring. Engineered driving interfaces.

Flybrain Drive connects a visual-circuit subgraph of MaleCNS v1.0 to a virtual car, prioritizing real-time interaction. The loop is: road state → engineered sensory encoding → neural spikes and synaptic propagation → engineered motor readout → vehicle motion.

Which data are real?

The source is Janelia MaleCNS v1.0: public neuron annotations, neurotransmitter predictions and connection-weight tables. Source SHA-256 checksums, type tables and compressed-model checksums are in the base data manifest and real-time circuit manifest. Data are licensed under CC BY 4.0; citation: Berg et al., 2026. This project selects, reindexes and compresses subgraphs.

The default circuit contains 8,000 neurons, 1,277,045 directed connections and 10,789,472 synapse counts. Alternatives contain 4,000 nodes with 523,173 connections, or the original 1,860 nodes with 114,188 connections. Each node retains its source body ID, type, transmitter and soma position. All selected nodes have recorded coordinates. Every retained edge and weight comes from the source; no fictional neurons or connections are added.

The 3D points use native MaleCNS EM coordinates in 8 nm voxels, with a shared translation, uniform scaling and display-orientation transform. This is neither a morphological reconstruction nor atlas registration. Gray soma points are anatomical context and do not all participate in the selected circuit. Up to approximately 4,000 edges are deterministically sampled from connections with weight at least 40, then drawn as straight lines between endpoints. They are not neurite paths. This display limit does not prune simulation connections.

How is the circuit selected?

Cholinergic T4a/T4b/T5a/T5b neurons with coordinates are divided into two spatial groups using the median x coordinate of all valid somas. Each group contributes 192 deterministically sampled inputs; another 128 LC4/LPLC2 inputs are sampled. For each group, the 260 targets with the greatest total direct output weight are included, followed by the 900 strongest merged second-hop targets. All original connections between selected nodes are retained.

The 4,000- and 8,000-node circuits retain these original 1,860 nodes and add downstream nodes with recorded coordinates, ranked by total outgoing synapse count from the original circuit. All three modes use the same body IDs at the driving interface. Each pool has 48 readout neurons distinct from injected inputs, and its group supplies at least 90% of their direct input weight from the three groups. “Left turn,” “right turn” and “braking” are assigned engineering roles, not validated biological driving functions. Background on motion and looming circuits: Klapoetke et al., Nature 2017 and Synaptic gradients transform object location to action, Nature 2023.

Dynamics and causal checks

Each neuron is a single-compartment, current-based LIF unit: 0.2 ms integration step, −52 mV rest/reset potential, −45 mV threshold, 20 ms membrane time constant, 5 ms synaptic time constant, 2.2 ms refractory period and 1.8 ms synaptic delay. Cholinergic connections are excitatory; GABA and glutamate are treated as inhibitory. Other transmitters have zero fast effect. These are assumed parameters, not a complete biophysical model calibrated neuron by neuron.

Inputs are deterministic, staggered pulses. Steering groups receive a 20 Hz baseline rising to 200 Hz with planned steering demand; braking input spans 0–150 Hz. Readout measures actual downstream mean firing rates with 65 ms smoothing. A piecewise-linear calibration table decodes steering demand, followed by an engineered actuator with 140 ms smoothing, a 0.005 rad deadband and a 0.9 rad/s rate limit. Brake-pool rate maps to brake force. Stimulus strength is never substituted for downstream spikes.

When all effective synaptic signs are set to zero in a test, input neurons still fire but downstream readout disappears and the car cannot start. Disconnecting neural motor output leaves the model running while the car brakes. Brain highlights use actual last-spike times with 120 ms (default), 500 ms or 1 s afterglow. Active counts measure neurons that fired at least once in that window; percentages use the selected simulated population as the denominator. A longer afterglow does not add spikes. Pause freezes time and highlights; reset clears them. The 139,659 gray reference points do not mean the whole brain is simulated. Charts show actual readout rates. Neural and vehicle dynamics share a clock; rendering is independent, and simulation speed is measured against wall time.

Real-time operation and circuit size

The default 8,000-neuron circuit targets 1× real time and measured approximately 1× in the local browser. If foreground performance stays below 0.9×, try 4,000 or 1,860 nodes. Changing size resets the drive and neural state. The page does not skip neural integration or invent spikes to maintain animation. A local full classified CNS run used 166,606 nodes and 25,574,615 connections, but an initial Node.js benchmark achieved approximately 0.39×, so the website does not load it by default. Local full-model experiment scripts remain available.

Other vehicles

Four conventionally controlled cars travel in both directions, waiting for signals, pedestrians and leading cars. They have no fly neural model. Approaching traffic increases the main car's brake-pathway input while a traffic supervisor limits speed. Oriented rectangular footprints approximate collisions. The traffic toggle acts immediately; pause and reset share the neural model's simulation clock.

Vehicle, cameras and limitations

The planner uses exact road centerlines and obstacle positions to construct paths and avoidance offsets. It does not recognize roads end to end from camera pixels. Eleven distance rays are centered on vehicle heading. The driver camera follows the car; the passenger camera is an observation view and does not change neural input. Neither recreates the physiology of fly compound-eye vision.

The car uses a simplified bicycle model, with grip affecting steering. Speed policy, road planning, encoding, decoding and collision stops are engineered. The fly appearance uses segmented meshes from a NeuroMechFly scan; its pose, color and foreleg grip are display animation with inverse kinematics. This female-derived body has not been registered neuron by neuron to the male MaleCNS brain and is not a musculoskeletal simulation. The Ferrari 458 Italia mesh uses its original steering wheel; foreleg contacts follow the same rim. The passenger view looks toward the driver. Pedestrians use four Quaternius characters with the author's Walk/Idle animations (CC0), moving along the models' +Z forward direction. Asset sources and licenses are retained.

This experiment does not show that a fly has learned to drive and is not suitable for real vehicles. Four signal-controlled crossing areas use staggered cycles of 18 seconds red, 22 seconds green and 4 seconds amber. Twenty pedestrians walk on sidewalks or crosswalks. Explicit traffic and pedestrian rules constrain speed while danger stimulates the neural brake pathway. Those rules are not learned traffic-law knowledge. Pedestrians and signals pause with the shared clock. Manually selecting green lights does not disable pedestrian yielding. High speeds or dense obstacles can cause stops or collisions.

Code uses the MIT license; Three.js retains its original MIT license. Neural model data remain CC BY 4.0. This page does not upload driving actions or neural activity.
